nameStory: The lanceleaf figwort gets its name from its narrow, lance-shaped leaves that taper to a point like a medieval weapon. The "figwort" part comes from an old belief that these plants could cure hemorrhoids, which were once called "figs" - though there's no actual medical connection to the Mediterranean fig fruit we know today.
description: Lanceleaf figwort is a tall, slender wildflower that can reach 3-6 feet high with a somewhat gangly appearance. It produces clusters of small, unusual brownish-red flowers that look almost like tiny snapdragons but with a more open, two-lipped shape. The plant has a square stem and opposite pairs of narrow, serrated leaves that give it a neat, orderly look. Despite its somewhat plain appearance, it's an important native wildflower that attracts various pollinators.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small brownish-red to greenish-purple flowers clustered in branched spikes, each flower about 1/4 inch long with two lips and a somewhat tubular shape - they feel papery when touched and have an unusual musty-sweet smell

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stem, with serrated edges that feel slightly rough to the touch and a prominent central vein

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall, upright plant reaching 3-6 feet with a square stem that feels distinctly four-angled when rolled between your fingers

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, round capsules that split open to release tiny dark seeds, making a subtle rattling sound when shaken in late summer

habitat: Lanceleaf figwort prefers moist to moderately dry soils in partially shaded areas like woodland edges, stream banks, and disturbed ground. You'll often find it along hiking trails, in clearings, or near old stone walls where the soil has been enriched. It tolerates a variety of soil types but seems to favor spots with some organic matter.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge in late spring with fresh green foliage. The distinctive opposite leaf arrangement and square stems become apparent as the plant begins its rapid upward growth.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from mid to late summer, when the small brownish flowers appear in terminal clusters. This is the best time for identification as both flowers and full foliage are present.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed capsules develop, turning brown and beginning to split open. Leaves may yellow slightly but often remain green well into fall.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to the ground, leaving only dried stems and seed heads that may persist. Look for the square, hollow stems as a winter identification clue.

funFact: Lanceleaf figwort flowers are specially designed for wasp pollination - their dull colors and musty scent specifically attract wasps rather than bees or butterflies, making this plant part of an exclusive wasp-only pollination club in the wildflower world.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other tall, square-stemmed plants like members of the mint family, but figworts lack the aromatic oils that give mints their distinctive smell when crushed. Memory trick: "Figworts are odor-free, mints smell minty to me."
contextualKnowledge: This species was once split into separate eastern and western varieties with different names (hare figwort and western figwort), which can cause confusion in older field guides. Modern botanists now recognize them as the same widespread species, so don't worry if you see different names in different books.
compareHints: Lanceleaf figwort differs from common figwort by having narrower, more lance-shaped leaves (rather than broadly oval ones) and generally growing taller and more slender. Late figwort blooms later in the season and has more rounded leaf bases, while lanceleaf figwort's leaves taper more gradually to their attachment point on the stem.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common figwort can be distinguished from late figwort by its more northern range and slightly smaller flowers, while lanceleaf figwort has much narrower, lance-shaped leaves rather than the broad, oval leaves of common figwort.
Late figwort blooms later than common figwort and grows taller, often reaching 8-10 feet versus common figwort's more modest 3-5 feet.
